issuer: New Mexico Taxation and Revenue Department
title: New Mexico TRD Ruling 100-96-3 Application of Section 7-1-26 to Estate
text:
Ruling 100-96-3
Issued: November 25, 1996
Effective: November 25, 1996
Revised: December 5, 2008, citations updated, as indicated by brackets
A ruling has been requested concerning the applicability of certain provisions of the Tax
Administration Act to the following facts:
X died September 5, 1992. The Co-Personal Representatives of X's estate (“Estate”)
filed a federal estate tax return and a New Mexico estate tax report in August 1993
and paid substantial estate taxes to both the Internal Revenue Service (“IRS”) and
the New Mexico Taxation and Revenue Department (“Department”).
The Estate filed its first fiduciary income tax return for a period ending July 31,
1993, paying the New Mexico fiduciary income tax due. A significant portion of this
tax represented capital gains from the sale of Estate assets. Pursuant to federal and
New Mexico law, the amount of gain was calculated by comparing the selling price
of the assets to the value of the assets on the date of X's death.
The IRS subsequently audited the Estate's federal estate tax return. After
determining that some estate assets had been undervalued, the IRS assessed
additional estate tax. The Co-Personal Representatives disagreed with the IRS's
determination of value and filed a petition in the United States Tax Court. That
petition is still pending.
If the IRS prevails, the Estate will owe additional estate taxes to the federal
government and to the State of New Mexico. At the same time, the Estate will be
entitled to a refund of federal and New Mexico income tax for the year ending July
31, 1993. This is because an increase in the date-of-death value of estate assets for
estate tax purposes will decrease the amount of capital gain the Estate must
recognize for income tax purposes.
In order to prevent its potential refund of income tax from being barred by the statute
of limitations, the Estate filed protective refund claims with the IRS and the
Department. In October 1996, the Department returned the refund claim with a
notice advising the Estate that New Mexico does not recognize protective claims.
The Estate asks whether the audit of the Estate's federal estate tax return qualifies as an
“audit” under NMSA 1978, Section 7-1-26(D) [7-1-26(F)], for purposes of extending the time
within which the Estate may file a claim for refund of New Mexico income tax paid for the year
ending July 31, 1993.
Pursuant to Section 7-1-26(B) [7-1-26(D)] NMSA 1978, no refund of tax may be allowed
unless the claim for refund is filed within three years of the end of the calendar year in which
payment of the tax was originally due. Under Subsection B [D], the statute of limitations for

claiming a refund of fiduciary income taxes due for the year ending July 1, 1993, would be
December 31, 1996.
Section 7-1-26(D) [7-1-26(F)] NMSA 1978 provides an extended limitations period for
refund claims based on adjustments of federal tax resulting from an IRS audit:
D. [F.] If, as a result of an audit by the internal revenue service ..., any
adjustment of federal tax is made with the result that there would have been an
overpayment of tax if the adjustment to federal tax had been applied to the taxable
period to which it relates, claim for credit or refund of only that amount based on the
adjustment may be made as provided in this section within one year of the date of
the internal revenue service audit adjustment or payment of the federal refund or
within the period limited by Subsection B [D] of this section, whichever expires later
…
Nothing in Subsection D [F] requires the IRS to audit the specific tax for which the refund
claim is made. Subsection D [F] does require that the claim be based on an adjustment of federal tax
resulting from an IRS audit and that the adjustment apply to the same taxable period for which the
New Mexico refund is sought.
In this case, any adjustment to the Estate's federal income tax liability for the year ending
July 31, 1993, will be a direct result of the IRS audit of the federal estate tax return. If the pending
estate tax litigation is decided in favor of the IRS, the Estate will be able to recover federal income
tax based on the increase in the date-of-death value of X's assets, which is also the basis of those
assets for income tax purposes. The refund of federal income tax will, in turn, trigger the one-year
statute of limitations contained in Subsection D [F] of Section 7-1-26.
Under the facts presented, the Estate will have one year from the date the IRS refunds any
federal income tax the Estate overpaid for the year ended July 31, 1993, within which to file a claim
for refund of New Mexico income tax overpaid for the same period.

issuer: New Mexico Taxation and Revenue Department
title: New Mexico TRD Ruling 100-94-1 Record Retention--CD ROM application
text:
Ruling 100-94-1
Issued: October 25, 1994
Effective: October 25, 1994
Revised: December 5, 2008, correction, as indicated by brackets
A ruling has been requested concerning the applicability of certain provisions of the Tax
Administration Act to the following facts:
X, a business in New Mexico, stores accounting and other records on CD-
ROM media, using computer scanning technology. The resulting CD-ROM files are
in unalterable form. The CD-ROM files are available for computer display and for
hard-copy printing. The printed documents are identified as copies but are otherwise
indistinguishable from the originals. The back-up copies of the CD-ROM disks are
made and originals documents are destroyed. The process is standardized as a
regular business practice across the company's divisions and facilities.
X requests a ruling on the acceptability of CD-ROM disks as the media for accounting and
other documents for tax compliance and audit purposes. X also asks how long it should retain
records for state tax purposes.
Section 7-1-10 NMSA 1978 states in part:
A. Every person required by the provisions of any statute administered
by the department to keep records and documents and every taxpayer shall maintain
books of account or other records in a manner that will permit the accurate
computation of state taxes or provide information required by the statute under
[which] he is required to keep records....
Under the provisions of Section 7-1-10 NMSA 1978, assuming that all relevant records are
stored, X's proposed method of record keeping is acceptable because the documents will be kept in
a manner that will permit the accurate computation of state taxes.
The Tax Administration Act sets no time requirement for taxpayer retention of books of
account or other records. The Department has no rule on this question. However, Section 7-1-18
NMSA 1978 sets out time limits on the Department's ability to assess tax asserted to be due.
Depending upon a taxpayer's situation, the Department may assess unpaid taxes for a period of up to
ten years.

issuer: New Mexico Taxation and Revenue Department
title: New Mexico TRD Ruling 355-94-1 Estate Tax: Nonresident
text:
Ruling 355-94-1
Issued: July 12, 1994
Effective: July 12, 1994
A ruling has been requested concerning the applicability of certain provisions of the Estate
Tax Act to the following facts:
X died in 1993 while a resident of another state. X and X's spouse owned property in
several states including New Mexico. X through X's will and estate planning
anticipated no taxes to New Mexico because of the federal unified credit.
Subsequent to filing an estate return for X in one of the other states (not the state in
which X was domiciled), a decision of that state's supreme court affecting the value
of X's property in that state may mean that X's estate now has a federal estate tax
liability.
X's representative asks if X will owe any New Mexico estate tax on income arising from the
property located out-of-state?
Section 7-7-2 NMSA 1978 defines "net estate" to mean "taxable estate" as defined in Section
2051 of the United States Internal Revenue Code.
Section 7-7-4 NMSA 1978 prescribes how estates of nonresidents who have property in
New Mexico are to be taxed. It states in part:
“A. Tax in an amount computed as provided in this section is imposed on
the transfer of the net estate located in New Mexico of every nonresident...
B. The tax shall be computed by multiplying the federal credit by a
fraction, the numerator of which is the value of the property located in New Mexico
and the denominator of which is the value of the decedent's gross estate.” (Emphasis
added)
...
D. The transfer of the property of a nonresident is exempt from the tax imposed
by this section to the extent that the property of residents is exempt from taxation under the
laws of the state in which the nonresident is domiciled.”
If the New Mexico estate tax applies at all to the value of a decedent's property in New
Mexico, Section 7-7-4(B) NMSA 1978 requires the estate tax be calculated for nonresidents as a
percentage of the federal Section 2011 credit. This is to avoid the fruitless debate over which asset or
assets triggered the federal tax liability. It is as equally valid to claim that the New Mexico assets are
to be added on top of the sum of the assets in the other states to determine which portion of the estate
bears the burden of the federal tax as it is to claim that the estate assets in another state are added to
New Mexico assets and that, therefore, only those out-of-state assets bear the federal tax. All assets
of a federally-taxable estate wherever located contribute proportionately to the size of the gross
estate and to the taxable portion.
X will have a New Mexico estate tax liability if the value of X's estate is such that a federal
Section 2011 credit arises unless the provisions of Subsection D of Section 7-7-4 NMSA 1978
apply.
If Subsection D does not apply, the New Mexico liability equals the maximum amount of the

federal Section 2011 credit for X's estate times a fraction, the numerator of which is the value of X's
New Mexico property and the denominator of which is the gross value of X's estate.
If the state in which X was domiciled exempts the transfer of the property of nonresidents
from that state's estate, inheritance or equivalent tax, then the transfer of X's New Mexico property
would be exempt from New Mexico estate tax pursuant to Subsection D of Section 7-7-4 NMSA
1978.

issuer: New Mexico Taxation and Revenue Department
title: New Mexico TRD Ruling 495-13-1 Film Credit for Production Services and Expenditures
text:
Ruling 495-13-1
Issued: January 25, 2013
Effective: January 25, 2013
A ruling has been requested concerning the applicability of certain provisions of the Film
Production Tax Credit to the following facts:
X is a corporation which is a film production company as defined by Section 7-
2F-2(G), NMSA 1978. X will contract with Y, a company that will provide
goods and perform certain specialty services in New Mexico for the production of
the film. Y will neither be owned by X nor affiliated with X. Y will also provide
facilities, equipment (including but not limited to grip and electrical equipment,
camera equipment, props, set dressing, wardrobe, picture vehicles, hardware and
expendables), transportation and other material or activities to X. The equipment
will be purchased or leased by Y from various sources including manufacturers,
distributors, or other third-party merchandisers of equipment, who may be outside
the State of New Mexico. This may include employing or lending the services of
its employees to the production through a lending and assignment agreement. Y
will have physical presence at all times during the production in the state of New
Mexico from which the vendor conducts business, stores inventory or otherwise
creates, assembles or offers for sale or lease the product or services. Y will
employ laborers that include at least one New Mexico resident, but may have
employees that are not New Mexico residents. Individuals performing services for
Y under the contract between X and Y may not be residents of New Mexico.
X asks whether the amounts paid by X to Y will qualify for the film production tax credit if:
(1) X will pay Y directly under the Production Services Agreement (PSA) for goods and
services provided for the production of a film in New Mexico;
(2) Y is a New Mexico limited liability company and will at all times have physical
presence in the state of New Mexico during the production;
(3) X certifies that the services and other direct production expenditures for which the
credit is claimed were performed or provided by Y in New Mexico.
(4) X is eligible for the credit under Section 7-2F-1(K) NMSA 1978;
(5) X does not deliver to Y a nontaxable transaction certificate pursuant to Section 7-9-
86, NMSA 1978;
(6) Y will employ laborers that include at least one New Mexico resident, but may have
employees that are not New Mexico residents; and
(7) Y will purchase or lease equipment from various sources or other third-party
merchandisers of equipment, who may be outside of the State of New Mexico.
Relevant Law
Section 7-2F-1(A)(1) NMSA 1978 states in part that the film production tax credit is available to
an eligible film production company for “direct production expenditures made in New Mexico
that: (a) are directly attributable to the production in New Mexico of a film or commercial

audiovisual product; (b) are subject to taxation by the state of New Mexico; (c) exclude direct
production expenditures for which another taxpayer claims the film production tax credit; and (d)
do not exceed the usual and customary cost of the goods or services acquired when purchased by
unrelated parties.”
Section 7-2F-1(L) NMSA 1978 states:
L. The division shall determine the eligibility of the company and shall
report this information to the taxation and revenue department in a manner and at
times the economic development department and the taxation and revenue
department shall agree upon. The division shall also post on its web site all
information provided by the film production company that does not reveal
revenue, income or other information that may jeopardize the confidentiality of
income tax returns, including that the division shall report monthly the projected
amount of credit claims for the fiscal year.
Section 7-2F-2(C) NMSA 1978 states:
C. “direct production expenditure”:
(1) except as provided in Paragraph (2) of this subsection, means a
transaction that is subject to taxation in New Mexico, including:
(a) payment of wages, fringe benefits or fees for talent,
management or labor to a person who is a New Mexico resident;
(b) payment to a personal services business for the services
of a performing artist if the personal services business: 1) pays gross receipts tax
in New Mexico on the portion of those payments qualifying for the tax credit;
and; 2) deducts and remits withheld income tax pursuant to Subsection I of
Section 7-3A-3 NMSA 1978; and
(c) any of the following provided by a vendor: 1) the story and
scenario to be used for a film; 2) set construction and operations, wardrobe,
accessories and related services; 3) photography, sound synchronization, lighting
and related services; 4) editing and related services; 5) rental of facilities and
equipment; 6) leasing of vehicles, not including the chartering of aircraft for out-
of-state transportation; however, New Mexico-based chartered aircraft for in-state
transportation directly attributable to the production shall be considered a direct
production expenditure; provided that only the first one hundred dollars ($100) of
the daily expense of leasing a vehicle for passenger transportation on roadways in
the state may be claimed as a direct production expenditure; 7) food or lodging;
provided that only the first one hundred fifty dollars ($150) of lodging per
individual per day is eligible to be claimed as a direct production expenditure; 8)
commercial airfare if purchased through a New Mexico-based travel agency or
travel company for travel to and from New Mexico or within New Mexico that is
directly attributable to the production; 9) insurance coverage and bonding if
purchased through a New Mexico-based insurance agent, broker or bonding
agent; and 10) other direct costs of producing a film in accordance with generally
accepted entertainment industry practice; and

(2) does not include an expenditure for:
(a) a gift with a value greater than twenty-five dollars ($25.00);
(b) artwork or jewelry, except that a work of art or a piece of
jewelry may be a direct production expenditure if: 1) it is used in the film
production; and 2) the expenditure is less than two thousand five hundred dollars
($2,500); or
(c) entertainment, amusement or recreation;
Section 7-2F-2(M) NMSA 1978 states:
M. "vendor" means a person selling goods or services that has a physical
presence in New Mexico and is subject to gross receipts tax pursuant to the Gross
Receipts and Compensating Tax Act [7-9-1 NMSA 1978] and income tax
pursuant to the Income Tax Act [7-2-1 NMSA 1978] or corporate income tax
pursuant to the Corporate Income and Franchise Tax Act [7-2A-1 NMSA 1978].
Ruling
Provided that X is an eligible production company under the provisions of Section 7-2F-1(K)
NMSA 1978, X will be eligible for the credit in the amount equal to the percentage specified in
Section 7-2F-1(B) NMSA 1978 of the direct production expenditures that meet the requirements
of Sections 7-2F-1(A)(1) and 7-2F-2(C) NMSA1978. If Y meets the definition of vendor in
Section 7-2F-2(M) NMSA 1978, then Y is a vendor for purposes of the film production tax
credit. If the services provided by Y to X are listed in Section 7-2F-2(C)(1)(c) NMSA 1978,
subject to gross receipts tax in New Mexico, and Y employs laborers (some of which must be
New Mexico residents as defined in the Income Tax Act), then the expenditures for the services
are eligible for the film production tax credit.
If the facilities, equipment (including but not limited to grip and electrical equipment, camera
equipment, props, set dressing, wardrobe, picture vehicles, hardware and expendables),
transportation and other material and activities provided by Y to X are listed in and meet the
requirements of Section 7-2F-2(C)(1)(c) NMSA 1978, and are subject to taxation in New
Mexico, then the expenditures are eligible for the film production tax credit. If X is an eligible
production company, then on the Form RPD-41229, Application for Film Production Tax Credit,
X must certify the qualifying direct production expenditures reported on the claim:
• include only expenditures made in New Mexico directly attributable to the approved
production;
• include only transactions which are subject to taxation by the State of New Mexico;
• exclude expenditures for which another taxpayer claims the film production tax
credit; and
• exclude expenditures for which the film production company delivered a nontaxable
transaction certificate pursuant to Section 7-9-86 NMSA 1978.
However, certification by X is not sufficient by itself. The New Mexico Film Division of the
Economic Development Department must determine eligibility of the company, pursuant to
Section 7-2F-1(L) NMSA 1978, and report this information to the Taxation and Revenue

Department. Moreover, as with all film credit applications, the Taxation and Revenue
Department will review invoices from Y to X and other documentation to determine whether
claimed expenditures meet statutory and regulatory requirements.

title: New Mexico TRD Ruling 495-12-1 Film Credit for Specialty Services Performed  in New Mexico for Film

Issued: March 20, 2012
Effective: March 20, 2012

issuer: New Mexico Taxation and Revenue Department
title: New Mexico TRD Ruling 495-07-2 Applicability of Technology Jobs Tax Credit
text:
Ruling No. 495-07-02
Issued: October 11, 2007
Effective: October 11, 2007
A ruling has been requested concerning the applicability of the New Mexico Technology Jobs
Tax Credit Act, NMSA 1978, Section 7-9F-1 et seq., to the following facts:
X is a research and development company that was founded in New Mexico and began
operating in 2001. The founders of the company invented a process of growing quantum
dots on substrates, from which they were attempting to develop marketable products.
Their development activities were funded through venture capital investors.
X applied for, and was approved for, the Technology Jobs Tax Credit by the New Mexico
Taxation and Revenue Department (hereafter, “Department”). X received three
successive credits -- $88,764.00, $115,183.00, and $103,103.00 on qualifying
expenditures made in 2002, 2003 and 2004, respectively. The credits were applied to
gross receipts, compensating and withholding tax liabilities on CRS-1 reports from
September 2003 through May 2006. Approximately 70% of the credit amounts claimed
was applied to withholding taxes. X has $51,299 of unused credit from the 2004
application.
The market for X’s technology has not sufficiently materialized and investors have
determined that they will cease funding the development activities in the near future. The
company is not relocating the business, but will likely sell its furniture and fixtures to an
unrelated company outside New Mexico. X’s intellectual property, if sold, will likely go
to a company outside NM.
X requests a ruling on the following questions:
1) Does Section 7-9F-11 NMSA 1978 apply to X, given the fact pattern outlined?
2) The term “cease operations” is not defined in Section 7-9F-3 NMSA 1978. How does the Department
define the term?
(a) If a taxpayer continues to exist as a legal entity in New Mexico and continues to comply with
all necessary tax filings, is this sufficient to not be deemed as “ceasing operations?”
(b) If not sufficient, what must the company do to continue its operations, especially given the
fact that the company has always been only a development-stage company?
3) If X does have to pay back the credit, would all of the credit used need to be paid back or is there some
ability to apportion the amount based on the length of time that has transpired from the initial credit
application and ultimate dissolution of the business?
4) Does the two-year requirement in Section 7-9F-11 NMSA 1978 begin running from the time the credit
is granted or from the time the credit is actually claimed on the appropriate form?
5) How would the Department enforce the recapture provision in Section 7-9F-11 NMSA 1978?
(a) Would the Department enforce this via audit assessment and eventual lien and levy?
(b) Could the Department enforce these provisions against the officers and investors of the
corporation?
(c) How is this impacted if the company filed for bankruptcy?

6) If X does sell some of its assets to a New Mexico company, will this constitute a “successor in
business” for purposes of Section 7-9F-11?
(a) If so, will the successor become liable for recapture of the credit?
(b) Is the answer different if the company acquiring the assets is not doing business in New
Mexico?
Question 1:
Section 7-9F-11 NMSA 1978 of the Technology Jobs Credit provides:
Recapture. If the taxpayer or successor in business of the taxpayer ceases operations in
New Mexico for at least 180 consecutive days within a two-year period after the taxpayer
has claimed a basic credit or an additional credit at a facility with respect to which the
taxpayer has claimed the basic credit or the additional credit, the department shall grant
no further basic credit or additional credit with respect to that facility. In addition, any
amount of approved basic credit not claimed against the taxpayer’s gross receipts tax,
compensating tax or withholding tax and any amount not claimed against the taxpayer’s
income tax or corporate income tax shall be extinguished, and within 30 days after the
180th day of the cessation of operations, the taxpayer shall pay the amount of any gross
receipts tax, compensating tax, or withholding tax for which an approved basic credit was
taken and any income tax or corporate income tax against which an approved additional
credit was taken.
X applied for and claimed the Technology Jobs Credit. If X does not continue to exist as a
technology company for two years after the last credit was claimed, X is subject to recapture.
Question 2:
The phrase “cease operations” is not defined within the Technology Jobs Tax Credit Act.
However, the Department is interpreting it to mean either: (1) to close a company’s qualifying facility,
from which it was conducting qualifying research and development, and no longer conduct business from
that location; or (2) to no longer engage in business in New Mexico due to the relocation of the enterprise
to another state; or (3) to no longer engage in business due to the complete dissolution of the enterprise.
Section 7-9F-3 NMSA 1978 states in part:
G. “qualified facility” means a facility in New Mexico at which qualified research is
conducted other than a facility operated by a taxpayer for the United States or any
agency, department or instrumentality thereof:
H. “qualified research” means research:
(1) that is undertaken for the purpose of discovering information:
(a) that is technological in nature; and
(b) the application of which is intended to be useful in the
development of a new or improved business component of the
taxpayer; and
(2) substantially all of the activities of which constitute elements of a process of
experimentation related to a new or improved function, performance, reliability
or quality, but not related to style, taste or cosmetic or seasonal design factors;

Legal existence is not sufficient basis and the plant must continue to operate a “qualified facility”
as defined in Section 7-9F-3(G) doing qualified research as defined in Section 7-9F-3(H).
Question 3:
Section 7-9F-11 states that, when a taxpayer ceases operations in New Mexico for at least 180
days within a two-year period after the taxpayer has claimed a credit, the taxpayer must pay the amount of
any gross receipts tax, compensating tax or withholding tax for which an approved credit was taken. X
last claimed a credit in 2006. Accordingly, if X ceases operation in New Mexico within a two year period
after 2006, X will have to pay all taxes for which it took a credit within 30 days after the 180th day of
cessation of operations.
Question 4:
The statute specifies that the two-year repayment period runs from the time the credit is claimed
against tax filings. X has submitted claims against CRS-1 forms from September 2003 to May 2006; the
Department would be able to verify the submission date of these reports and the corresponding claim
dates. Each month’s claim stands on its own in relevance to recapture.
Question 5:
The instructions for the Technology Jobs Tax Credit application specify the terms of the
recapture. Therefore, the Department expects X to give notice upon closure of their New Mexico facility.
The Department would then issue an assessment for the amount of the gross receipts, compensating and
withholding tax due in accordance with the recapture statute. The Department can hold the officers of the
corporation personally liable for the payment of the withholding taxes. The Department would continue
with audit and collections efforts regardless of whether X files for bankruptcy, as allowed by the
Bankruptcy Code.
Question 6:
Subsection C of Section 7-1-61 NMSA 1978 for successor in business states in part:
If a person liable for any amount of tax from operating a business transfers that business
to a successor…the successor shall pay the amount due to the department…
Regulation 3.1.10.16 NMAC for determination of successor in business states:
A. The following indicia are used by the secretary or secretary’s delegate as
factors in determining whether a business is a successor:
(1) Has a sales and purchase of a major part of the materials, supplies,
equipment, merchandise or other inventory of a business enterprise occurred
between a transferor and a transferee in a single or limited number of
transactions?
(2) Was a transfer not in the ordinary course of the transferor’s business?
(3) Was a substantial part of both equipment and inventories transferred?
(4) Was a substantial portion of the business enterprise that had been
conducted by the transferor continued by the transferee?
(5) By express or implied agreement did the transferor’s good will follow
the transfer of the business properties?
(6) Were uncompleted sales, services or lease contracts of the transferor
honored by the transferee?

(7) Was unpaid indebtedness to suppliers, utility companies, service
contractors, landlords or employees of the transferor paid by the transferee?
(8) Was there an agreement precluding the transferor from engaging in a
competing business to that which was transferred?
B. If one or more of the indicia mentioned above are present, the secretary or
secretary’s delegate may presume that ownership of a business enterprise has transferred
to a successor in business.
If they are a successor and they continue the qualified activities in New Mexico, the Department
will treat the transferee as a successor who will become liable for the recapture of the credit in accordance
with Section 7-9F-11.

issuer: New Mexico Taxation and Revenue Department
title: New Mexico TRD Ruling 495-96-1 Basis of Qualified Equipment for Investment Credit
text:
Ruling 495-96-1
Issued: October 15, 1996
Effective: October 15, 1996
A ruling has been requested concerning the application of certain provisions of the Investment
Credit Act to the following facts:
X is regularly engaged in manufacturing in New Mexico both end products and the
processing equipment necessary to manufacture the end products. The manufacturing takes
place in facilities consisting of real property, improvements and equipment, all of which is
owned by a New Mexico political subdivision (Z) and leased to X under authority of an
industrial revenue bond. The processing equipment which X manufactures is both for use in
X's own end product manufacturing plants and for sale to third parties.
As agent for Z, X has purchased machines, mechanisms and components (“Parts”)
and fabricated and assembled the manufacturing equipment in place within the plant. To
establish the value of the manufacturing equipment or components of the manufacturing
equipment for federal income tax purposes, X capitalized the direct and indirect costs of the
Parts and of the installation, assembly and fabrication of the Parts into the integrated
manufacturing equipment. The capitalized cost of the manufacturing equipment or
components included all direct and indirect costs which are includable in capital
expenditures under the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 for property which is depreciable as
3-, 5-, 7-, 10- or 15-year property thereunder and includes tangible property, materials,
supplies, tools, scraps, spoilage, administration, purchasing, transportation, warehousing,
handling, security, insurance, legal, accounting, rework, permits, carrying charges, taxes and
similar services and expenses incurred in connection with the purchase and production of
the manufacturing equipment.
In 1991, the Taxation and Revenue Department issued Ruling No. 495-91-1 to X
allowing qualified equipment to be valued at its capitalized value for federal income tax
purposes in this situation. (It also addressed other issues.) The law subsequently changed to
incorporate this part of the ruling.
In a corporate reorganization, X has formed a new corporation, Y, and has
contributed to Y all of X's rights, title and interest in the property used by X in its end
product manufacturing operation and its process equipment manufacturing operations. The
contribution of assets to Y was consistent with the provision of the Internal Revenue Code
found at 26 USCA Section 351. Following this Section 351 occurrence, Y will carry on the
manufacturing operations in New Mexico and elsewhere, using the same property and
employees as were previously used by X.
Y requests that Ruling 495-91-1 which was originally issued to X be re-issued to Y. Because of
changes in the provisions of the Investment Credit Act which took effect subsequent to the issuance of
Ruling 495-91-1 and because some provisions of the Investment Credit Act will not apply to Y, the
department cannot issue a verbatim re-issuance of Ruling 495-91-1, but instead will rule on the above facts
as they apply to Y under the current provisions of the Investment Credit Act.
Y asks if the value of qualified equipment for purposes of the Investment Credit Act is the same as
the basis of valuation for federal income tax purposes, which includes all of the capitalized direct and
indirect costs of the machines, mechanisms, tools and components and installation, assembly and

fabrication thereof into integrated manufacturing equipment or components thereof. Y further inquires if
qualified equipment includes all 3-, 5-, 7-, 10- and 15-year property under the Internal Revenue Code which
is an essential machine, mechanism or tool, or a component or fitting thereof, used directly and exclusively
in the manufacturing plant, including by way of example, such things as process equipment, lights, boilers,
air conditioners, computers and peripherals, furniture, office equipment, air compressors, water chillers,
refrigeration equipment, water treatment equipment, packaging equipment, warehousing equipment and
electrical control equipment.
Under Section 7-9A-6 NMSA 1978:
Equipment not previously used in New Mexico and not previously approved for a
credit under the Investment Credit Act that is owned by the taxpayer or owned by ... the
state or a political subdivision thereof and leased or subleased to the taxpayer is qualified
equipment if it is in New Mexico and is incorporated or to be incorporated within one year
into a manufacturing operation. (emphasis added)
Qualified equipment includes any “essential machine, mechanism or tool, or a component or fitting
thereof, used directly and exclusively in a manufacturing operation and subject to depreciation for purposes
of the Internal Revenue Code by the taxpayer carrying on the manufacturing operation...”. (Section 7-9A-3
NMSA 1978). Accordingly, such items as furniture, shelving and supplies are not “equipment”. [3 NMAC
13.6.9 (formerly IC 6:2)]
Because the term manufacturing operation is defined as a plant to produce goods, equipment need
not be employed exclusively in the manufacturing process to be qualified equipment as long as the
equipment is employed in the plant in which the manufacturing process occurs. Therefore for the purposes
of the Investment Credit Act, “equipment” may include, but is not limited to, such items as manufacturing
process equipment, lights, boilers, air conditioners, computers and peripherals, air compressors, water
chillers, refrigeration equipment, water treatment equipment, packaging equipment, warehousing equipment
and electrical control equipment if such items are used directly and exclusively in the plant. [3 NMAC
13.6.10 (formerly IC 6:3)]
The value of qualified equipment until January 1, 1998 “... shall be the adjusted basis established for
equipment under the applicable provisions of the Internal Revenue Code”. (Section 7-9A-7 NMSA 1978)
But, effective January 1, 1998, Section 7-9A-7 NMSA 1978 states:
The value of qualified equipment shall be the purchase price of the equipment unless
the equipment is introduced into New Mexico and has been owned for more than one year
prior to its introduction into New Mexico by the taxpayer applying for the credit, in which
case the value shall be the reasonable value of the equipment at the time of its introduction
into New Mexico; provided that no taxpayer shall for any taxable year claim a value of
qualified equipment greater than two million dollars ($2,000,000).
Because the statute which takes effect January 1, 1998 does not provide any direct guidance on
valuation of self-constructed machinery and equipment, Y proposes using its capitalized value. Y asserts the
capitalized value for purposes of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 for self-constructed machinery and
equipment is analogous to “purchase price” for machinery and equipment bought from another party.
Hence, the department will accept the capitalized value for purposes of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986
as the basis for Investment Credit Act valuation of self-constructed machinery and equipment installed in
the New Mexico manufacturing plant.

This ruling does not address nor does it intend to address the issue of whether X may transfer or
assign any unclaimed or unused portion of an investment credit earned by X to Y.

issuer: New Mexico Taxation and Revenue Department
title: New Mexico TRD Ruling 495-97-1 Withholding Agent and Investment Credit Act
text:
Ruling 495-97-1
Issued: April 10, 1997
Effective: April 10, 1997
A ruling has been requested concerning the applicability of certain provisions of the
Investment Credit Act, NMSA 1978, Sections 7-9A-1 (1995 Repl. Pamp.), to the following
facts:
X is a corporation doing business in New Mexico. X has carried on a
manufacturing operation in New Mexico in facilities consisting of real
property, improvements and equipment that are owned by a New Mexico
political subdivision and leased to X under the authority of an industrial
revenue bond. In the course of its business, X has applied for and been
granted approval of investment credits on equipment used in its
manufacturing operation.
X has formed a new corporation, Y, in a corporate reorganization. X has
contributed to Y all of its rights, title and interest in the property used in New
Mexico's manufacturing operation. Y will carry on the manufacturing
operations in New Mexico using the same property and employees that were
previously used by X. As part of the reorganization, X applied for and was
granted authority to act as withholding agent for Y under the provisions of
Internal Revenue Code § 3504.
As Y's authorized withholding agent, X will control the payment of wages
and remit the payment of withholding tax for all of Y's employees. Under the
provisions of IRC § 3504, X will be equally liable with Y for payment of
employment tax on Y's employees, including interest and penalties, if
applicable.
X asks whether it may apply its approved, but unused, investment credits against
withholding tax X pays on behalf of Y as Y's withholding agent.
Section 7-9A-8(A) of the Investment Credit Act allows “a taxpayer” who has
applied for and been granted investment credits to claim those credits against “the taxpayer's
compensating tax, gross receipts tax or withholding tax due to the state of New Mexico”.
The issue to be determined is whether X, the taxpayer who has been granted investment
credits, may apply those credits against Y's state withholding tax liability.
Section 7-3-2(C) of the Withholding Tax Act defines “employer” to include “a
person, or an officer, agent or employee of that person, having control of the payment of
wages...”.
Section 7-3-11(A) provides:
When a fiduciary, agent or other person has the control, receipts, custody or
disposal of or pays the wages of an employee or group of employees
employed by one or more employers and the fiduciary, agent or other person

has been designated by the United States secretary of the treasury to perform
such acts as required of employers for federal withholding purposes under
the Internal Revenue Code, the fiduciary, agent or other person shall perform
the acts required of employers by the provisions of the Withholding Tax Act.
All provisions of Chapter 7 NMSA 1978 applicable in respect to an
employer shall be applicable to a fiduciary, agent, or other person so
designated, but the employer, unless provided otherwise by law, for whom
the fiduciary, agent or other person acts shall remain subject to the
provisions of Chapter 7 NMSA 1978 applicable to employers.
The Withholding Tax Act treats any person with control over the payment of wages,
including a person designated as a withholding agent under IRC § 3504, as an employer
liable for payment of withholding tax. When X pays withholding tax on wages paid to Y's
employees, X is satisfying its own, as well as Y's, liability for payment of tax. This meets
the requirement in Section 7-9A-8(A) that a taxpayer holding investment credits claim those
credits against “the taxpayer's ... withholding tax due to the state of New Mexico”.
X may apply its approved, but unused, investment credits against withholding tax X
pays on behalf of Y.

issuer: New Mexico Taxation and Revenue Department
title: New Mexico TRD Ruling 495-07-1 Film Production and High Wage Job Tax Credits
text:
Ruling 495-07-1
Issued: April 4, 2007
Effective: April 4, 2007
A ruling has been requested on the application of the film production tax credit governed
by Chapter 7, Article 2F NMSA 1978 to the following facts:
X is in the business of creating and developing visual effects, animation and
computer graphics for its own productions as well as for third-party motion
picture and other media production entities. X provides these effects services to
these entities in lieu of them having to develop such services internally. In these
situations, X effectively acts as a production company for significant portions of
each film or production.
X enters into agreements with third-party production entities to develop and
produce visual effects, animation and the like for motion picture productions,
marketing materials, commercials and other media projects. Although much of
the effects services are performed after completion of principal and ongoing
photography, X employees and staff are usually involved in all stages of any film
production, which could also include preproduction, previsualization, principal
and ongoing photography. X directly and independently is responsible for all of
its personnel and contractors, hardware, software and other equipment and
materials, as well as for all overhead, rentals, leases and any other production
requirements that may or may not be unique to a particular production.
X is evaluating the possibility of expanding its facilities to provide opportunities
for personnel and productions to develop a presence in New Mexico and avail
itself of state tax incentives, thereby reducing production costs. To that end, X
plans to set up and maintain a significant business presence in New Mexico. X
would relocate certain employees to New Mexico and would need to hire
additional staff to be located in New Mexico. X would also need to make
significant purchases related to hardware, software and other infrastructure
necessary to create a fully operational production environment in New Mexico.
X asks:
1. Does X qualify as a “film production company” within the meaning of Section 7-2F-2(E),
and may X apply for a film production tax credit?
2. Will the visual effects, animation, performance capture, computer graphics and other
services that X provides within New Mexico be treated as “postproduction” activities
within the meaning of Section 7-2F-2(F), including the labor and other costs that X incurs
throughout the production of a film?

3. Will the wages and related fringe benefits paid to employees of X for services rendered in
New Mexico qualify as taxable postproduction expenditures regardless of the residency
status of the employees?
4. Will payments by X to a third-party vendor for postproduction services in New Mexico
qualify as taxable postproduction expenditures that may be included in X’s measure of
the film production tax credit, provided that X does not deliver a Type 16 NTTC to the
third-party vendor?
5. May X contractually limit the right of another film production company to claim the film
production tax credit when postproduction expenditures are incurred by X in New
Mexico on behalf of the other film company?
6. If X receives a Type 16 NTTC from another film production company, will X be
precluded from including all of X’s postproduction expenditures in the computation of
the film production tax credit?
7. If X hires eligible employees to perform qualified research in New Mexico, will X be
able to claim the technology jobs tax credit provided by Section 7-9F-1 through 7-9F-9
NMSA 1978, even if the related wage and benefit expenditures are also included with
X’s measure of the film production tax credit?
8. Assuming that X is an eligible employer who hires eligible employees in new high-wage
economic-based jobs, would X be able to claim the applicable high-wage jobs tax credit
provided by Section 7-9G-1 NMSA 1978, even if the wage and benefit expenditures are
also included within X’s measure of the film production tax credit?
Response to Question 1:
Under Chapter 7, Article 2F NMSA 1978, an eligible film production company may
claim a credit against personal or corporate income taxes based on expenditures related to the
production of a commercial film. A “film production company,” for purposes of the film
production tax credit, is defined as “a person that produces one or more films.” See Section 7-
2F-2(E) NMSA 1978. The statute does not define the term “produces”. Nevertheless, the credit
may be claimed for direct production expenditures and postproduction expenditures that are
“directly attributable” to the production of a film. See Section 7-2F-1(A)(1) & (2). This suggests
that, for purposes of the credit, producing a film involves both direct production and
postproduction activities. Thus, a company, such as X, that performs postproduction services,
qualifies as a “film production company” and may apply for the credit.
Response to Question 2:
For periods prior to July 1, 2007, a “postproduction expenditure” is defined as:

an expenditure that occurs after the completion of principal and ongoing
photography, including an expenditure for editing, Foley recording, automatic
dialogue replacement, sound editing, special effects, including computer-
generated imagery or other effects, scoring and music editing, beginning and end
credits, negative cutting, soundtrack production, dubbing, subtitling or addition of
sound or visual effects; but not including an expenditure for advertising,
marketing, distribution or expense payments.
Section 7-2F-2(F) NMSA 1978.
For periods after July 1, 2007, a “postproduction expenditure” is defined as:
an expenditure for editing, Foley recording, automatic dialogue replacement,
sound editing, special effects, including computer-generated imagery or other
effects, scoring and music editing, beginning and end credits, negative cutting,
soundtrack production, dubbing, subtitling or addition of sound or visual effects;
but not including an expenditure for advertising, marketing, distribution or
expense payments.
Laws 2007, Chapter 172, Section 4.
For periods prior to July 1, 2007, X’s expenditures related to the production of a film
after the completion of principal and ongoing photography for visual effects, animation,
performance capture, computer graphics and similar services in New Mexico, including labor
and other costs, will constitute postproduction expenditures for purposes of claiming the film
production tax credit. Expenditures for the same services that are made during or after the
completion of principal and ongoing photography may be used for purposes of calculating the
credit only if they meet the criteria for direct production expenditures under Section 7-2F-2(B)
NMSA 1978.
For periods after July 1, 2007, X’s expenditures related to the production of a film that
occur before, during and after the completion of principal and ongoing photography for visual
effects, animation, performance capture, computer graphics and similar services in New Mexico,
including labor and other costs, will constitute postproduction expenditures for purposes of
claiming the film production tax credit.
Response to Question 3:
To qualify as a “direct production expenditure” for purposes of the film production tax
credit, wages and fringe benefits must be paid to a New Mexico resident. See Section 7-2F-
2(B)(1). In contrast, none of the expenditures included in the definition of “postproduction
expenditure” are limited by residency. Thus, wages and fringe benefits X pays an employee for
postproduction services performed in New Mexico may be used to calculate the credit regardless
of the employee’s residency status.
Response to Question 4:

The film production tax credit may not be claimed with respect to otherwise covered
direct production and postproduction expenditures “for which the film production company has
delivered a nontaxable transaction certificate pursuant to Section 7-9-86 NMSA 1978.” Section
7-2F-1(D). Section 7-9-86 provides a deduction from taxable gross receipts for receipts from
selling property or services to a qualified production company, as defined in that section, that
delivers a nontaxable transaction certificate, known as a Type 16 NTTC, to the seller.
Payments made by X to a third-party vendor for postproduction services performed in
New Mexico may be used to calculate the amount of the film production tax credit, provided the
payments meet the definition of postproduction expenditure and X does not deliver a Type 16
NTTC to the vendor. By the same token, a vendor that did not receive a Type 16 NTTC from X
would not be entitled to deduct its receipts from the transaction, even if the vendor otherwise met
the requirements of Section 7-9-86.
Response to Question 5:
The Taxation and Revenue Department does not have the authority to determine the
validity of a contract between two private parties that limits the parties’ rights to claim the film
production tax credit. However, as made clear in recent amendments to the law governing the
credit, the same qualified direct production or postproduction expenditure may not be used by
more than one film production company to calculate the film production tax credit, and the
Taxation and Revenue Department would not approve two claims for the film production tax
credit based on the same postproduction expenditures. See Section 7-2F-1(A) NMSA 1978 (as
amended by Laws 2007, Chapter 172, Section 3).
Response to Question 6:
As discussed above in response to Question 4, a film production company is prohibited
from claiming the film production tax credit for expenditures for which it has delivered a Type
16 NTTC. The prohibition does not apply if a film production company receives a Type 16
NTTC. If X receives a Type 16 NTTC from another film production company, X will not be
precluded from using its postproduction expenditures to calculate the film production tax credit.
Response to Question 7:
The Technology Jobs Tax Credit Act, Sections 7-9F-1 to -12 NMSA 1978, provides for a
credit against gross receipts tax, compensating tax or withholding tax. The credit is based on
expenditures made by technology-based businesses engaging in certain research and
development activities. See Sections 7-9F-2, 7-9F-5. Whether X could qualify for the
technology jobs tax credit is beyond the scope of this ruling, but, assuming X met the statutory
requirements for that credit, nothing in the Technology Jobs Tax Credit Act or Chapter 7, Article
2F would preclude X from claiming the technology jobs tax credit in addition to the film
production tax credit.
Response to Question 8:

Under Section 7-9G-1 NMSA 1978, eligible employers may claim a credit against gross
receipts tax and similarly collected taxes that is based on wages and benefits paid to employees
in newly created high-wage jobs. Whether X could qualify for the high-wage jobs tax credit is
beyond the scope of this ruling, but, assuming X met the statutory requirements for that credit,
nothing in Section 7-9G-1 or Chapter 7, Article 2F would preclude X from claiming the high-
wage jobs tax credit in addition to the film production tax credit.
The above responses are based on the facts presented and law at the time the ruling was
drafted. Any subsequent change to the facts or law may also change the Department’s responses
to questions addressed in the ruling.

issuer: New Mexico Taxation and Revenue Department
title: New Mexico TRD Ruling 495-12-2 Film Credit for Specialty Services Performed in New Mexico for Film
text:
Ruling 495-12-2
Issued: October 24, 2012
Effective: October 24, 2012
A ruling has been requested concerning the applicability of certain provisions of the Film
Production Tax Credit to the following facts:
X is a limited liability company which is a film production company as defined by
Section 7-2F-2(G), NMSA 1978. X will contract with Y, a company that will
perform certain specialty services in New Mexico for the film and television
industry. Y will neither be owned by X nor affiliated with X. Y will also provide
facilities, equipment, transportation or other material or activities to X. This may
include employing or lending the services of its employees to the production
through a lending and assignment agreement. Y will have physical presence in
the state of New Mexico from which the vendor conducts business, stores
inventory or otherwise creates, assembles or offers for sale or lease the product or
services. Y will employ laborers that include at least one New Mexico resident,
but may have employees that are not New Mexico residents. Individuals
performing services for Y under the contract between X and Y may not be
residents of New Mexico.
X asks whether the amounts paid by X to Y will qualify for the film production tax credit if:
(1) X is eligible for the credit under Section 7-2F-1(K) NMSA 1978;
(2) X does not deliver to Y a nontaxable transaction certificate pursuant to Section 7-9-
86, NMSA 1978; and
(3) X certifies that the services and other direct production expenditures for which the
credit is claimed were performed or provided by Y in New Mexico.
Section 7-2F-1(A)(1) NMSA 1978 states in part that the film production tax credit is available to
an eligible film production company for “direct production expenditures made in New Mexico
that: (a) are directly attributable to the production in New Mexico of a film or commercial
audiovisual product; (b) are subject to taxation by the state of New Mexico; (c) exclude direct
production expenditures for which another taxpayer claims the film production tax credit; and (d)
do not exceed the usual and customary cost of the goods or services acquired when purchased by
unrelated parties.”
Section 7-2F-2(C) NMSA 1978 states:
C. “direct production expenditure”:
(1) except as provided in Paragraph (2) of this subsection, means a
transaction that is subject to taxation in New Mexico, including:
(a) payment of wages, fringe benefits or fees for talent,
management or labor to a person who is a New Mexico resident;

(b) payment to a personal services business for the services
of a performing artist if the personal services business: 1) pays gross receipts tax
in New Mexico on the portion of those payments qualifying for the tax credit;
and; 2) deducts and remits withheld income tax pursuant to Subsection I of
Section 7-3A-3 NMSA 1978; and
(c) any of the following provided by a vendor: 1) the story and
scenario to be used for a film; 2) set construction and operations, wardrobe,
accessories and related services; 3) photography, sound synchronization, lighting
and related services; 4) editing and related services; 5) rental of facilities and
equipment; 6) leasing of vehicles, not including the chartering of aircraft for out-
of-state transportation; however, New Mexico-based chartered aircraft for in-state
transportation directly attributable to the production shall be considered a direct
production expenditure; provided that only the first one hundred dollars ($100) of
the daily expense of leasing a vehicle for passenger transportation on roadways in
the state may be claimed as a direct production expenditure; 7) food or lodging;
provided that only the first one hundred fifty dollars ($150) of lodging per
individual per day is eligible to be claimed as a direct production expenditure; 8)
commercial airfare if purchased through a New Mexico-based travel agency or
travel company for travel to and from New Mexico or within New Mexico that is
directly attributable to the production; 9) insurance coverage and bonding if
purchased through a New Mexico-based insurance agent, broker or bonding
agent; and 10) other direct costs of producing a film in accordance with generally
accepted entertainment industry practice; and
(2) does not include an expenditure for:
(a) a gift with a value greater than twenty-five dollars ($25.00);
(b) artwork or jewelry, except that a work of art or a piece of
jewelry may be a direct production expenditure if: 1) it is used in the film
production; and 2) the expenditure is less than two thousand five hundred dollars
($2,500); or
(c) entertainment, amusement or recreation;
If X is an eligible production company under the provisions of Section 7-2F-1(K) NMSA 1978,
X will be eligible for the credit in the amount equal to the percentage specified in Section 7-2F-
1(B) NMSA 1978 of the direct production expenditures that meet the requirements of Sections 7-
2F-1(A)(1) and 7-2F-2(C) NMSA1978. Y is a vendor for purposes of the film production tax
credit. If the services provided by Y to X are listed in Section 7-2F-2(C)(1)(c) NMSA 1978,
subject to gross receipts tax in New Mexico, and Y employs laborers (some of which must be
New Mexico residents as defined in the Income Tax Act), then the expenditures for the services
are eligible for the film production tax credit.
If the facilities, equipment, transportation or other materials and activities provided by Y to X are
listed in and meet the requirements of Section 7-2F-2(C)(1)(c) NMSA 1978, and are subject to
taxation in New Mexico, then the expenditures are eligible for the film production tax credit. If X
is an eligible production company, then on the Form RPD-41229, Application for Film
Production Tax Credit X must certify the qualifying direct production expenditures reported on
the claim:

• include only expenditures made in New Mexico directly attributable to the approved
production;
• include only transactions which are subject to taxation by the State of New Mexico;
• exclude expenditures for which another taxpayer claims the film production tax
credit; and
• exclude expenditures for which the film production company delivered a nontaxable
transaction certificate pursuant to Section 7-9-86 NMSA 1978.
However, certification by X is not sufficient by itself. As with all film credit applications, the
Department will review invoices from Y to X and other documentation to determine whether
claimed expenditures meet statutory and regulatory requirements.

issuer: New Mexico Taxation and Revenue Department
title: New Mexico TRD Ruling 225-94-1 Severance Pay
text:
Ruling 225-94-1
Issued: January 21, 1994
Effective: January 21, 1994
Revised: December 12, 2008, correction and citation updated, as indicated by brackets
A ruling has been requested concerning the applicability of certain provisions of the Income
Tax Act to the following facts:
X was a resident of Texas until August of 1991. Until June 1991 X, was employed
by Company Y. In June, 1991 Y closed the division in which X was employed. X
was granted a severance package. X received the severance pay over a twelve month
period including the last half of 1991 and the first half of 1992. In August 1991, X
moved to and became a resident of New Mexico.
X states that the severance pay received while a resident of New Mexico is not subject to
taxation under the Income Tax Act since the severance pay was for wages earned in Texas prior to
becoming a resident of New Mexico. X references the instructions for completing the Personal
Income Tax Returns which state “Only income earned while a New Mexico resident is subject to
New Mexico income tax.”
Section 7-2-3 NMSA 1978 states:
A tax is imposed at the rates specified in the Income Tax Act upon the net income
of every resident individual and upon the net income of every nonresident individual
employed or engaged in the transaction of business in, into or from this state or
deriving any income from any property or employment within this state. (Emphasis
added)
Section 7-2-11(A)(3) NMSA 1978 states "compensation of a resident [taxpayer] shall be
allocated to this state."
Taxation and Revenue Department regulation IT 11:6 [3.3.11.11(A) NMAC] states: “All
compensation received while a resident of New Mexico shall be allocated to this state whether or
not such compensation is earned from employment in this state.”
Except for accrual basis taxpayers which X does not claim to be, income generally is
“earned” for income tax purposes in the period in which it is received, not the period in which the
activity, if any, which gave rise to the income occurred. X's severance pay is reportable as
compensation in the year in which it was received. Severance pay received after X became a
resident of New Mexico is subject to the New Mexico income tax.
The New Mexico income tax imposes a tax on the total income of a resident unless there is a
specific exemption or deduction provided in the New Mexico Income Tax Act. In this case there is
no specific deduction or exemption which would authorize X to exclude the severance pay.

issuer: New Mexico Taxation and Revenue Department
title: New Mexico TRD Ruling 225-98-1 Spouses With Different States of Residency: Allocation of Income
text:
Ruling No. 225-98-1
Issued: April 21, 1998
Effective: April 21, 1998
A ruling has been requested concerning application of certain provisions of the Income
Tax Act to the following facts:
T has been a New Mexico resident for several years. In September 1997, T takes a
job in another state, with the intention of moving to that state. T’s spouse,
however, remains in New Mexico to sell their New Mexico residence. Eventually
the spouse decides against moving. T is able to secure a transfer from T’s
employer to a New Mexico location near T’s New Mexico residence. T moves
back to New Mexico in January 1998.
Both New Mexico and the other state are community property states.
T asks whether T may allocate to the other state the income T earned from employment
in the other state in 1997.
T is married. T’s spouse never left New Mexico and apparently had no intention of
changing domicile at the end of the 1997 taxable year. Thus, assuming T can demonstrate
evidence of an intent at the end of the 1997 taxable year to make the other state T’s domicile, T
is a nonresident for New Mexico income tax purposes and T’s spouse is a resident.
Because T’s spouse is a resident and New Mexico is a community property state, all of
T’s income is subject to the Income Tax Act.
Section 7-2-11 NMSA 1978 of the Income Tax Act, however, states in part:
7-2-11. TAX CREDIT--INCOME ALLOCATION AND APPORTIONMENT.--
A. Net income of any individual having income that is taxable both
within and without this state shall be apportioned and allocated as follows:
...
(4) compensation of a nonresident taxpayer shall be allocated
to this state to the extent that such compensation is for activities, labor or personal
services within this state; provided, if the activities, labor or services are
performed in this state for fifteen or fewer days during the taxpayer's taxable year,
the compensation may be allocated to the taxpayer's state of residence....
Therefore, T’s compensation from T’s employment in the other state from September
1997 through the end of that year may be allocated to the state in which T was employed.
